**Quality comparisons:** Pairwise quality judgments were often skipped (most evals had 0 pairs evaluated, marked skipped) so little quality-comparison data exists for 3 of 5 evals. Where comparisons were made: in "cross-reference-overlap-per-account" (3 pairs), with_skill was favored more often (7 vs 2, especially on completeness), at medium confidence. In "critical-ta-findings-error-only" (only 1 pair evaluated), results were mixed, with without_skill favored on actionability/completeness and with_skill on accuracy — but this rests on just one comparable pair, so it's a weak signal.

**Runtime and cost:** Results are mixed and not large enough on their own to be decisive. In two evals without_skill was slightly faster/cheaper (e.g., 37s/$0.31 vs 43s/$0.36; 29s/$0.24 vs 32s/$0.27). **Overall picture:** The most consistent and well-supported signal across this set is that with_skill matched the expected output more often and passed more assertions, particularly those involving structural correctness (section presence, account ID inclusion, ordering, and sourcing of counts), with higher output-run-to-run consistency and generally higher confidence ratings behind these judgments. without_skill was occasionally faster/cheaper and was favored in some individual quality sub-criteria (actionability, completeness) in the one eval with usable pairwise data, and quality-comparison data is largely absent (skipped) for most evals, limiting how far any single number can be generalized. Looking at individual criteria, with_skill was favored on completeness in all 3 pairs, and had a slight edge on accuracy (2 vs 1) and actionability (2 vs 1). This is a consistent but not overwhelming tilt toward with_skill's output quality, and the medium confidence means this should be read as a moderate rather than certain signal.

None of the runs exceeded the runtime threshold for either variant. Context window utilization was low and similar for both (4.9% vs 4.2%), with no compaction events for either.

Overall picture: On core correctness measures (expected output, assertion pass rates) the two variants are tied, including sharing the same failure mode on the "no invented overlaps" assertion. Where they diverge is that with_skill was faster, cheaper, showed slightly higher quality ratings (particularly completeness), and was somewhat more consistent across runs, while without_skill took longer and cost more and showed a bit more run-to-run variability. These quality and consistency signals are directionally in favor of with_skill but rest on medium-confidence judgments, so they should be treated as a moderate-confidence tradeoff rather than a decisive difference.
